slot.brief: Definite integral of f(x)/(f(x)+f(a−x)) type; apply King's property to halve the integral and evaluate at level 4 difficulty.

verdicts.working: Under x→π/2−x, the two numerator terms average to [2+x²+(π/2−x)²]/2, so the integral is 1/2∫₀^{π/2} dx/(2+sin²(2x)/4) = ∫₀^π dt/(8+sin²t), using t=2x. The standard integral gives π/√(8·9)=π/(6√2).

working:
Let $I$ denote the integral. Under $x\mapsto\frac{\pi}{2}-x$, the first factor becomes its complement and the other factor is unchanged; hence $2I=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{dx}{(1+\sin^2x)(1+\cos^2x)}$.\nWith $t=\tan x$, this integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{1+t^2}{(1+2t^2)(2+t^2)}\,dt=\frac13\int_0^\infty\left(\frac1{1+2t^2}+\frac1{2+t^2}\right)dt=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}$.\nTherefore $I=\dfrac{\pi}{6\sqrt2}$.

Independent check: Under x→π/2−x, the two numerator terms average to [2+x²+(π/2−x)²]/2, so the integral is 1/2∫₀^{π/2} dx/(2+sin²(2x)/4) = ∫₀^π dt/(8+sin²t), using t=2x. The standard integral gives π/√(8·9)=π/(6√2).
solution:
Under $x\mapsto \frac{\pi}{2}-x$, the rational factor averages with its complement to $\frac12$, so
$$I=\frac12\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{dx}{(1+\sin^2x)(1+\cos^2x)}.
$$
Setting $t=\tan x$ gives the integral on the right as $\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}$; hence $I=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{6\sqrt2}}$.
